claims.text: TEM can be used to characterize the microstructure of high-entropy alloys.
In situ HRTEM with an integrated heating stage enables atomic-scale investigation of the thermal behavior of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
In situ HRTEM can directly observe temperature-induced atomic rearrangements in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
In situ HRTEM can directly observe phase transformations in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
The initial AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are nearly equiatomic.
The initial AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles have a disordered solid-solution structure at room temperature.
Controlled heating will be applied inside an aberration-corrected TEM.
The experiment will use high-vacuum or inert-gas conditions and a calibrated incremental heating stage.
Heating induces atomic lattice distortions and phase transitions that change local atomic order.
Thermal energy overcomes atomic diffusion barriers in the nanoparticles.
Overcoming diffusion barriers causes atomic rearrangements.
The thermally induced atomic rearrangements may produce ordering phenomena or phase transitions.
Real-time observation can link configurational entropy and sluggish diffusion to elevated-temperature structural stability.
Atomic-scale imaging will reveal local ordering or phase transformation during heating.
The observed rearrangements will correlate with enhanced thermal stability relative to predictions based solely on thermodynamic contributions.
The room-temperature baseline has no visible phase transitions under static conditions.
Electron-beam irradiation may induce structural effects that can be confused with intrinsic thermal effects.
Reaching extremely high temperatures may compromise TEM image resolution.
The temperature at which measurable rearrangements or phase transitions occur is uncertain and may require calibration.

Failure to observe atomic rearrangement, diffraction changes, or phase transformations above expected activation thresholds would falsify the proposed ability of in situ HRTEM to resolve thermal behavior.
